As a result, most data center operators rely on local potable water resources because access to rainfall, grey water and surface water is seen as unreliable [23]. 3.2.1 Climate Weather and climate can significantly impact the energy efficiency and operational costs for a data center. One simple metric to measure climate is evaluating the average temperatures in a region of interest. This will affect the data center cooling efficiency over the course of a year [13]. Building facilities in cool, low-humidity regions provides cooling technology options that may not be feasible in warmer climates. This will lower energy costs, improve cooling efficiency and reduce environmental impact [3]. Within a region of interest, locations at a higher altitude may be preferable to a location in a lower altitude. 3.2.2 Indirect and Direct Water Use The US is a global leader in the data center industry, with more than 5,300 facilities, according to information from Statista.com, a global data and business intelligence platform. The round-the-clock operation of these data centers makes the digital world possible. In the process, data centers consume enormous amounts of resources, especially water. That water is used in two primary ways: indirectly, to generate the electricity to run the computer server equipment, and directly, as the medium to dissipate the heat generated by the servers and other data center equipment [14]. Within a data center, water is used for cooling server equipment rooms. Most data centers use a chilled water circuit to absorb the heat generated by the server equipment. The water is chilled by cooling units powered by electricity or, sometimes, by cool air from the outside using an air-cooled system [15]. When air cooled systems can be used in place of water-cooled systems, during periods of colder weather for example, water-cooled technologies become more efficient [16]. In some locations, water usage only commences when external temperatures rise above a certain threshold, increasing the need for cooling. Under such conditions, some data centers will start a system that sprays droplets of water (adiabatic cooling) to cool down the air flow by a few additional degrees before switching to a water chiller system [15]. A metric of data center water requirements is the water usage effectiveness (WUE). The WUE is the ratio between water used at the data center and electricity delivered to the server hardware [12].
